doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: Taking commissions and wanting guidelines
summary: He asks about a group's talent and limits before writing commissions.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: If you get a call to do a commission, are there guidelines that you like to get. For instance, if someone says I have a big band, write something for me, that’s very wide open.
Is it harder to do it that way than to say you know I really could use a Latin chart and we have a strong trumpet section?

Yeah I don’t want to say it’s harder. I would say there’s a higher chance — a greater chance that what I do may not fit this person’s group. If they say we don’t care, just write something, and they give me no limitations, I’m going to write for my own band and then give them the chart. They’ll pay me for it, and then I’ll play it with my group and record it. You know? So I usually require guidelines. Because I want everyone to be happy and I want the word of mouth to be that we asked him to write something, it came out great and it was perfect for our group. You know? So I usually ask about the talent in the group and the limitations and who the soloists are, what stylistically the band can handle, things like that. And so far I’ve hit the mark on all of them, but occasionally you’ll get a director who maybe has a loftier impression of what his group is, and maybe bites off a little more than he can chew for his group, you know, saying that they could do something when they’re really not prepared to do that. But I always kind of take things with a grain of salt, depending on how confident the director sounds when he’s saying all these things. But in general the ultimate goal is that I write something for them that they’re happy with and that I also get to play it with my group. It kills two birds with one stone.
